A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MBOK research by the same authors. Their main text, figures, tables, equations, code examples, proofs, and remaining appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching relocated material.

before.justification: v1 reports original MBOK perplexity, zero-shot accuracy, training ablations, kernel-allocation experiments, and generated examples in Section 6 and Appendix E.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds kernel-allocation visualization and measured GPU latency results, including Tables 11–12.

M1.justification: Successive SVID extraction, multiple Boolean kernels, Boolean optimization, last-kernel finetuning, distillation objectives, and the kernel-allocation algorithm remain unchanged. Algorithms 1–9 are retained. New hardware explanations and BitBLAS benchmarking do not establish a changed MBOK procedure.

E1.justification: Both use WikiText2 and C4, the same BoolQ, PIQA, HellaSwag, Winogrande, and ARC tasks, and the same generation prompts. Added comparisons and latency measurements concern existing model families and layers; they do not introduce new data domains or language-task requirements.

E2.justification: v2 adds reported comparisons with QuIP and ShiftAddLLM in Table 8, AWQ, BitStack, and DB-LLM in Table 9, and QuIP# and QTIP in Tables 10–12. AWQ was previously cited but not evaluated in these comparisons. The fixed-kernel comparator in v1 Figure 8 is also omitted from the corresponding v2 allocation plot.

E3.justification: v2 introduces an A100 layer-latency protocol using batch size 1, FP16 activations, two Boolean kernels, and specified matrix dimensions. Section 6 revises the stated Boolean learning rate from 5 × 10^3 to 5 × 10^-3. Table 6 relabels the final LLaMA2-13B row from two to three kernels without changing scores. These reported setting revisions do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: The allocation analysis changes: v2 Figure 9 adds a layerwise kernel-allocation profile at a 3.5-bit average, while Figure 10 drops v1's direct fixed-versus-allocated comparison. The existing kernel-count, kernel-training, latent-weight, and distillation-loss studies, along with generation examples, are retained.

E5.justification: Figure 5 retains its existing error-bar displays without new statistical explanation. Neither version documents experimental seed counts, repeated-run counts, or formal confidence/significance procedures. The added latency tables report point estimates without introducing uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: The benchmark scores in Tables 2, 3, 5, and 6 are retained, but Tables 8–12 add substantial comparison and runtime results. Table 10 reports QTIP perplexities of 6.52/7.99 versus MBOK's retained 6.83/8.53 on WikiText2/C4. Tables 11–12 report MBOK layer speedups of 2.14×–8.70× over FP16. These additions do not demonstrate an improvement over v1's MBOK performance.

T1.justification: New Appendix F derives multiplication counts for latent-weight and Boolean training, including a claimed 66.7% reduction in FP16–FP16 multiplications when Boolean operations are ignored. This adds a limited complexity analysis. The Boolean calculus, SVID propositions, and their proofs remain substantively unchanged; Appendix B largely restates existing algebra.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: direct Boolean-domain finetuning without latent weights, successive knowledge transfer, flexible kernel allocation, and favorable accuracy/compression and computational efficiency. New benchmark and hardware evidence supports these existing claims rather than redefining them.

C2.justification: v2 removes v1's acknowledgment that allocation fails to improve over fixed kernels and its warning that finetuning can undermine initialization-based allocation. Section 6.5 instead emphasizes deployment flexibility and interprets layerwise allocations through compression sensitivity. Appendices B, F, and G.7 add substantial hardware-efficiency explanations and attribute vector-quantization latency to encoding/decoding overhead.

D1.justification: Appendix B adds guidance on binary arithmetic versus native Boolean implementation. Appendix G.7 identifies BitBLAS, FP16/INT1 computation, A100 hardware, and official baseline implementation links. Existing core code examples and the twelve-V100 experimental disclosure are retained. The new reproducibility statement does not announce a new MBOK code release.

R1.justification: Sections 2 and G.6–G.7 substantially expand positioning against BitStack, DB-LLM, QuIP, ShiftAddLLM, QuIP#, and QTIP. v2 explicitly presents scalar quantization as the closest comparison class and distinguishes its training and hardware properties from vector quantization. This extends the research positioning beyond the accompanying switch to author-year citations.

P1.justification: v2 extensively rewrites the abstract and passages on knowledge transfer, allocation, experimental setup, ablations, and complexity. The allocation narrative is substantially replaced. The appendix structure expands around new hardware and complexity sections and closing ethics, reproducibility, and LLM-use statements, while the main section sequence remains recognizable.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 8–12 and the allocation-profile Figure 9, expands Table 1, and redraws the budget plot without the fixed-kernel series. Existing memory and distillation-loss figures are retained under new numbers. A different document template changes title treatment, headings, running headers, citation colors, table sizing, and code-block typography throughout.

improvement.justification: v2 strengthens practical efficiency evidence with measured A100 latency and broadens comparison against relevant methods. However, it removes v1's direct allocation comparison and substantive allocation limitations. New Table 8 also leaves bit-width/value assignments unexplained: OPT-350M's 23.12 appears under two bits although Table 3 assigns it to three kernels, and Table 8 does not identify its dataset or metric. These reporting weaknesses and lost qualifications prevent a reliable net quality judgment despite the useful additions.
